title: Data in support of the hPOP Human Proteomics project
projectDescription: A long-standing aspiration in multi-omics is to comprehensively understand how genetic and geographical factors shape phenotypic expression at the molecular, cellular and organismal level - ultimately revealing how the interplay between an organism's molecular landscape and its environment manifests in observable traits. While high-throughput multi-omics technologies have revolutionized our understanding of disease states, relatively few studies have explored molecular variation within and across healthy populations, especially with full-spectrum molecular data, leaving a significant knowledge gap. To address this gap and enhance our understanding of human molecular diversity, we conducted an analysis of 322 nominally healthy individuals from diverse ethnic backgrounds, integrating (1) deep multi-omic profiling - including genome sequencing, transcriptomics, glycomics, targeted and untargeted metabolomics, lipidomics, proteomics, 16S microbiota sequencing, metaproteomics, metallomics, and metabolic hormone and pathogen profiling, (2) clinical data collection, and (3) comprehensive lifestyle surveys. Our integrative analysis revealed three key findings: associations between molecular profiles (transcripts, proteins, metabolites, lipids, and microbiota) and phenotypic categories such as diet and age among healthy individuals; ethnicity-specific genetic polymorphisms in key genes governing whole-body homeostasis, particularly in lipid/carbohydrate metabolism and neuroinflammation pathways; and variation in the abundance of key proteins such as the TERF2 interacting protein (TERF2IP)  which is critical for cellular aging, genome stability, and protection against chromosomal degradation. These findings hold significant translational value, particularly in understanding ethnicity as a risk factor for autoimmune diseases. Many ethnicity-associated molecules identified in our study interact with existing therapeutic drugs, highlighting the potential need for ethnicity-specific drug dosing adjustments. Furthermore, our results suggest that geographical factors influence ethnic patterns, which may, in turn, affect longevity. Male individuals with European ancestry exhibited a lower phenotypic age, while those of Asian ancestry showed a higher phenotypic age when living outside their ancestral regions. By providing both a comprehensive baseline dataset of multi-omic variation in healthy individuals and critical insights into the molecular basis of human diversity, our study establishes a foundation for future precision medicine approaches and enhances our understanding of how environmental and genetic factors influence phenotypic and molecular traits.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Plasma (unfractionated; plasma pool samples, NIST standard samples) were prepared by the uSP3 method (PMID: 31137935) by dilution to approximately 2.5µg/µl in lysis buffer (1%SDS in 100 mM AmBic, 10 mM TCEP, 40 mM 2-CAA, pH 8.5) in 96 well plate format using an Opentrons OT-2 liquid handling system (Opentrons labworks Inc., NY, USA ). Samples were heat denaurated in the plates for 5 minutes at 95°C. A total of 10ul of the lysate (nominal 25ug) were transferred to new plate. A total of 5 µl SP3 beads (PureCube Carboxy MagBeads (50.000.000 beads/µl stock) were added to the lysate. A total of 15µl 100% acetonitrile (ACN) were mixed by pipetting, and proteins are left to bind at RT for 15 min. Beads are immobilized by OT-2 magnet and the supernatant is removed, and beads are washed twice with 200 µl of 80% ethanol (EtOH) and one time with 180 µl of 100% ACN. Beads were resuspended in 35 µl of digest solution (Promega Tryp/LysC mix; enzyme:protein ratio of 1:50) followed by digestion for 4 hours at 37°C and 600 rpm in a Thermomixer. Samples are acidified by adding 5 µl of 5% TFA and shaken for 5 min at 600 rpm. Beads are immobilized on a magnetic rack, and peptides recovered by transferring the supernatant to new plate. The samples were dried by vaccum centrifugation and resuspend in 25 µl loading buffer (0.1%FA, 0.1%TFA, 2% ACN) and the protein concentration measured by fluorescence assay (Pierce Quantitative Peptide Assays). MS injection-ready- samples were stored at -80°C. Plasma (Lipid-vesicle enriched; plasma pool samples, NIST standard samples) were prepared by the MagNET method (PMID: 38617345) using an Opentrons OT-2 based on automation script “MagNet enrichment and on-bead digestion with Evotip loading,v1.0” (Evosep Biosystems, Odense, Denmark). Neat plasma (10 μL) were mixed 1:1 by volume with Binding Buffer (BB, 100 mM Bis-Tris Propane, pH 6.3, 150 mM NaCl). MagReSyn® strong anion exchange magnetic microparticles (ReSyn Biosciences) and equilibrated 2 times in Equilibration/Wash Buffer (WB, 50 mM Bis Tris Propane, pH 6.5, 150 mM NaCl) with gentle agitation and then combined in a 1:4 ratio (volume beads to volume starting plasma) with the plasma:BB sample for 45 minutes at room temperature. The beads were washed with WB 3 times for 5 minutes with gentle agitation. The enriched membrane particles on the beads were then solubilized and reduced in 50 mM Tris, pH 8.5/1% SDS/10 mM Tris (2-carboxyethyl) phosphine (TCEP). Samples were alkylated with 15 mM chloroaceamide for 30 minutes. The samples were processed using protein aggregation capture (PAC) with minor modifications (PMCID: PMC6495262). Briefly, the samples were adjusted to 70% acetonitrile, mixed with washed PAC beads (Resyn MagReSyn hydroxyl beads (20 mg/ml)), and then incubated for 10 minutes at room temperature to precipitate proteins onto the bead surface. The beads were washed 3 times in 95% acetonitrile and 2 times in 70% ethanol for 2.5 minutes each on magnet. Samples were digested for 1 hour at 45 °C in 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate with trypsin-LysC mixture (Promega) at a ratio of 1:50 trypsin to protein. The digestion was quenched to 0.5% trifluoracetic and peptide digests stored at −80°C until LC-MS/MS analysis. Analytical Platform and Data Acquisition Quantitative label free liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis were performed on an EvosepONE (Odense, Denmark) coupled to a CaptiveSpray nanoelectrospray ionisation source (ZDV 20nm emitter, Bruker, Billerica, MA) and a timsTOF Pro2 mass spectrometer (Bruker, Billerica, MA). Peptide samples were loaded on Evotip Pure (Evosep Biosystems, Odense, Denmark) using an automated OT-2 Evotip Loading Protocol, v1.3. A total of 200ng peptide were used from each sample and analysed by the 60SPD LC-MS fractionation speed. In-between QC standards (200ng Hela tryptic digest Thermo Scientific Pierce; Biognosys iRT). The mass spectrometer was operated in positive ionization mode with data-independent acquisition and parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation (diaPASEF-long gradient) enabled. Sample QCs were automatically analysed using the ProteoScape GPU based search engine.
dataProcessingProtocol: Protein identification and quantification was performed using directDIA+ with default settings (global normalization by median; LFQ QUANT2.0 MS1) in Spectronaut v19.5 (Biognosys, Schlieren, CH). Raw files were matched against the UniProt human reference proteome (UP000005640 human reference proteome; gene count 20,596). Decoys and proteins that were identified based on less than two peptide sequences were removed. The resulting data was imported in Perseus (v 2.1.3.0) for log2-transformtion, averaging of duplicate runs (only plasma samples) and imputation of missing values from a normal distribution to mimic signal of low-abundant proteins only when using principle component analysis.
